newsitem.title: UGANDA: Zaire revolution good for business, Uganda says.
newsitem.headline: Zaire revolution good for business, Uganda says.

text.p: Business executives said on Saturday Laurent Kabila and his rebel forces would help Uganda's sagging economy by bringing order to eastern Zaire and pushing back Ugandan guerrillas.

"It is the best thing that has happened to Uganda in a long time. This is going to be a great opportunity for Ugandan goods and business in the region. I foresee the Ugandan economy booming in the near future," said Mike Mukula, chairman of the Uganda Exporters and Importers Association.

"I think Kabila will bring order. We want to trade normally, not harassed by immigration officials who haven't been paid in ages. It is good for regional cooperation," said Agard Didi, former managing director at the Uganda Milling Company.
Political commentators said civil strife in southeastern Uganda was virtually ended with the advance of Kabila's rebels because Ugandan dissidents had been pushed far from the border.
Kabila's rebels, who took up arms in October, control half of Zaire, including its economic heartland with its diamond, copper, cobalt and gold mines.

Kabila's administration has cut taxes on Ugandan goods by 70 percent sparking an influx of Ugandan products in rebel-held areas. Business leaders say Zairean gold, diamonds, timber and coffee have all started trickling into Uganda.
Last month, Ugandan Finance Minister Jehoash Mayanja Nkangi said civil wars in northern and southeastern Uganda had cut trade and undermined Ugandan manufacturing.

On Friday, Planning and Economic Development Minister Richard Kaijuka forecast gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 1996/97 at 6.3 percent, lower than a target of 7.0 percent or the 8.5 percent growth attained in the previous year.
On Tuesday, Minister of State for Economic Monitoring Syda Bumba said: "According to what is on the ground, the economy has not performed very well. In fact, it was a downward trend."

Ugandan manufacturers previously complained that the border fighting meant that sales of soap, cooking oils, plastics, detergents, cigarettes, cement and steel were down because markets in southeastern and northern Uganda and eastern Zaire were not accessible.
Alykhan Marmali, executive director of leading Ugandan manufacturer Mukwano Industries, said increased trade in those former no-go areas would help the Ugandan economy immensely.
Kaijuka said expanding trade into Zaire would help non-coffee exports rise to $257 million in 1996/97 from $196 million in the previous year (July/June).

Kaijuka said manufacturing production in January was 30.7 percent higher than in January 1996 while the average sector growth for the first seven months of 1996/97 compared with the same period in the 1995/96 was 22.9 percent.
"Basically, production should go up. There is demand in eastern Zaire and southern and northern Uganda are more accessible now," a business consultant in Kampala said.
